Detention has little effect on deterrence, can harm youth and goes against children’s rights as outlined in the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, a document that guides the U.S. The United States joined the treaty in 1995, among the first countries to do so. Nevertheless, the U.S. repeatedly declined to ratify a protocol intended to penalize parents for sending their children on dangerous trips to the U.S. To halt additional suffering, we must, at the very least, adhere to the initial convention. And we must make sure we release kids who are eligible for reunification with their families.
Juvenile justice reform is in many ways a mirror of the immigration tragedy. Mass incarceration has racial undertones, resulting in the greatest proportion of Black youth in prison and the highest instances of detained children against their benefit due to three-strikes laws. In immigration, youth from El Salvador, Guatemala, and Honduras have been abducted, abused, assaulted, and tormented by gangs, forced to dwell in fear and observe family members murdered or otherwise harmed. Children cannot move across borders in harm’s way.
Mass incarceration is random, removing from an entire group of young individuals their chance for education and increasing their likelihood of falling into a criminalized life path. In immigration, the arbitrary use of the term “child” cannot be justified. Too many children, including babies, are detained. The arbitrary remedy is to make sure that no child who legitimately qualifies as a child is subjected to detention.
Mass incarceration is based in punishment and deterrence, its physical setting reflecting the moral truth of the individual being punished. Conversely, an older prisoner is seen as more deserving of punishment, while a younger child is considered more innocent and not deserving of jail time.
